<reason>A wins by making full scientific opportunity cost the decisive comparison and honestly acknowledging that reallocation would sacrifice some crewed capabilities. B raises a legitimate fixed-cost objection but never establishes why preserving worthwhile capabilities requires majority funding. B also repeatedly alleges that A excludes sample quality and physiology despite A explicitly counting them, and evades the hypothetical about superior robotic science. A’s justification for the scale of reallocation remains underdeveloped, preventing a dominant win, but its comparative reasoning and responses are substantially stronger.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A turns B’s infrastructure objection: an expensive standing capability must justify the discoveries forgone to maintain it; its high fixed costs do not themselves establish budgetary priority. A’s closing also directly corrects B’s claim that it charges the entire architecture against just one sampling mission.</best_rebuttal>
